warmup.q: A merchant requests a refund; the dashboard reloads from a follower that is 300 ms behind, shows no refund, and the merchant clicks Refund again. Which change fixes this for every merchant at the lowest cost?
options: Make replication synchronous to every follower
Remember the log position of each user's last write, and read from a follower only once it has replayed that far, otherwise from the leader
Add more followers so each one has less load and less lag
Cache the dashboard for a second so reloads are faster
warmup.why: Only this merchant's own write is missing, so only this merchant's reads need to wait or go to the leader, and only until the follower catches up. Synchronous replication to every follower would fix it by making every commit wait for the slowest follower. More followers don't bound lag. A cache serves an even older answer. (The duplicate refund itself should also be stopped by an idempotency key; that protects the money, not the screen.)

sections.h: Followers are behind, and behind has no upper bound
sections.html:
The merchant dashboard of a payment processor sends 90% of its queries to three followers, so the leader keeps its CPU for card authorizations. Lesson 1 showed why those followers must be asynchronous: waiting for three followers on every commit would make the slowest one set every payment's latency. So the dashboard reads the past. Usually it is a few milliseconds old. During a burst of writes, a long-running replay, a vacuum conflict (lesson 4) or a slow network link, it can be seconds or minutes old, and nothing in the protocol puts a limit on it.

If the writes stopped, every follower would catch up and agree with the leader. That is all eventual consistency promises: the copies converge eventually, and "eventually" comes with no number. Asynchronous followers of PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle are eventually consistent in exactly the way people associate with NoSQL stores.

Keep lesson 1's picture: one log with positions, and each follower at some position in it. Add one rule: a read served by a follower returns the data as of that follower's position. Lag is the distance between the leader's position and the follower's, and every database will tell you what it is:

  • PostgreSQL, on the primary: pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) in pg_stat_replication, in bytes, and replay_lag in time.
  • MySQL: Seconds_Behind_Source in SHOW REPLICA STATUS, an estimate in seconds.
  • MongoDB: rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo() in mongosh, per secondary.
  • Redis: the master's master_repl_offset minus each replica's offset, in INFO replication.

Stale data on its own is often fine: a sales total that is two seconds old surprises nobody. Trouble starts when a reader already knows about something newer than the follower it is reading. Each of the three anomalies in this lesson is a read served at a position behind something the reader has already done or seen. Each fix is the same move in a different form: the reader carries a position, and refuses to read below it.

try.title: Positions over time
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. A payment is captured every 100 ms until 2,000 ms; r1 is 20 ms behind the leader and r2 900 ms behind. It prints each node's log position and whether r2 can see pay-15.
Predict when r2 first shows pay-15, which the leader committed at 1,500 ms. Then run it with -Pargs='lag 2500' and say how long "eventually" is now.

code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l03.demo.AnomaliesDemoKt -Pargs='lag' -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l03.demo.AnomaliesDemoKt -Pargs='lag 2500' -q

try.expect:
a payment captured every 100 ms; r1 is 20 ms behind, r2 is 900 ms behind
    time   leader         r1         r2             pay-15 on r2
  500 ms        5          4          0                not there
 1000 ms       10          9          1                not there
 1500 ms       15         14          6                not there
 2000 ms       20         19         11                not there
 2500 ms       20         20         16                 captured
 3000 ms       20         20         20                 captured
once the writes stop at 2,000 ms, both followers converge: that is all "eventually consistent" promises

r2 shows pay-15 from 2,400 ms, 900 ms after the commit. A lag in time becomes a lag in positions that depends on the write rate: 900 ms behind is 9 payments at this rate and would be 9,000 at a busy one. With a 2,500 ms lag, r2 is still at 0 at 2,500 ms and at 5 at 3,000 ms; it reaches 20 at 4,500 ms, after the table ends and long after the last write.

sections.h: Read your own writes: carry the position of your last commit
sections.html:
At 1,000 ms a merchant requests a refund for pay-41. The leader commits it at position 2. At 1,010 ms the dashboard reloads, and the load balancer sends the query to follower r1, 300 ms behind and still at position 0. The refund list is empty. The merchant, sure the click didn't work, clicks Refund again. The idempotency key stops a second refund in the database, but the screen was wrong, and the support ticket is real.

The guarantee this merchant needs is read-your-writes (also called read-after-write): after you write something, your own reads always show it. It says nothing about other people's reads. There are four ways to get it, from blunt to precise.

  1. Read anything the user can change from the leader: their own refunds, their profile, their settings. Simple and correct, until most pages show the user's own data and the leader takes most reads again.
  2. Read from the leader for a fixed time after each of the user's writes, say one minute. This covers normal lag, but not a follower that is ten minutes behind after a restart.
  3. Carry the position. When the write commits, the application keeps its log position as the session's token. Before reading on a follower, the router compares the follower's position with the token: at or past it, read there; behind it, wait a little or go to the leader. On PostgreSQL, the token is pg_current_wal_lsn() read just after the commit, and the check on the standby is pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= token (PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adds a WAIT FOR LSN command for the waiting). MySQL's equivalent is the GTID set of the write and WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET. MongoDB builds it in: a causally consistent session remembers the operation time of its last write, sends it with each read as afterClusterTime, and a secondary waits until it has applied that far. The MongoDB manual guarantees this only with majority read and write concern.
  4. Make the commit wait: synchronous_commit = remote_apply returns only once a standby has replayed the commit (lesson 4). Every read there is fresh, and every commit pays for it.

Option 3 is usually the right one. It sends to the leader only the reads that would be wrong, and it measures freshness by position, not by the clock. Two costs come with it. The token must live where every request of that user can find it: a cookie works for one browser, but a merchant who refunds on a phone and checks on a laptop needs the token stored server-side against the user. And a follower that never catches up (paused, broken, far behind) must not hold a request forever, so bound the wait and fall back to the leader.

try.title: Lose your own refund on a real standby, then check the position
steps: Start the primary and its standby from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait. Open psql on each in its own terminal: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the session below, switching terminals at each comment. pg_wal_replay_pause() freezes the standby's replay, so the lag is as long as you want and the result is the same every time.
Replace 0/5003FD0 with the my_write your primary printed. Before the first comparison on the standby, predict received and replayed: which one has passed your write?

code.title: psql on the standby and on the primary
code.html: -- standby SELECT pg_wal_replay_pause(); -- primary INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (2, 1200, 'duplicate', now()) RETURNING refund_id; SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS my_write; -- standby SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 2 AND amount_minor = 1200; SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() AS replayed, pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() AS received, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '0/5003FD0' AS has_my_write; SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume(); SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '0/5003FD0' AS has_my_write; SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 2 AND amount_minor = 1200;

try.expect:
On fresh servers the refund is id 7 and my_write is 0/5003FD0 (yours may differ). The standby can't see it:

 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
(0 rows)

 replayed  | received  | has_my_write
-----------+-----------+--------------
 0/5000000 | 0/5004000 | f
(1 row)

The standby has received the WAL past your write (0/5004000) and replayed none of it: replay is paused. The comparison says f, so a router would send this read to the primary. Right after pg_wal_replay_resume(), the comparison can still say f for a moment, as it did in this run, because replay takes a few milliseconds to restart. A moment later the refund is there:

 has_my_write
--------------
 f
(1 row)

 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1200
(1 row)

That moment is why real code waits a bounded time and checks again, rather than checking once. Leave the servers running for lesson 4, or stop them with docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v.

sections.h: Monotonic reads: never move backwards in time
sections.html:
Payment pay-9 was authorized at 0 ms and captured at 1,000 ms. An operator in the payments team keeps its page open and reloads it. Two followers serve the page: r1 is 20 ms behind, r2 is 900 ms behind, and the load balancer alternates between them. At 1,100 ms r1 shows captured. At 1,150 ms r2 shows authorized. At 1,200 ms r1 shows captured again. The capture appears, disappears and comes back, and an operator who acts on the second screen might capture the payment a second time.

The operator wrote nothing, so read-your-writes has nothing to say here. The missing guarantee is monotonic reads: once you have seen some state, your later reads never show an older one. Time may stand still for you, and it never runs backwards. It is weaker than "everyone sees the latest data" and stronger than eventual consistency.

The classic fix is sticky routing: pick each user's follower from a hash of the user id, and send all of that user's reads there. One follower's position only moves forward, so neither do the user's reads. It costs uneven load when some users read much more than others, and it breaks exactly when you need it most: when the sticky follower dies, the user moves to another follower, which may be behind the first one. The lab reproduces that: a user sees captured on r1, r1 dies, the next read on r2 says authorized.

The precise fix is the previous section's token, with one more rule. The session remembers the highest position any of its reads was served at, and the router never serves it below that (or below its own last write). A sticky follower is tried first, so most reads stay where they were, and a dead or lagging one is skipped for any follower at or past the token, or for the leader. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions give monotonic reads this way, as part of the same majority/majority guarantee.

try.title: Count the steps back in time
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. It reloads pay-9 six times, first round-robin across r1 and r2, then routed with a session token.
Before you run it with -Pargs='monotonic 40', where r2 is only 40 ms behind: will round robin still go back in time? Why does a smaller lag not make the anomaly impossible?

code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l03.demo.AnomaliesDemoKt -Pargs='monotonic' -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l03.demo.AnomaliesDemoKt -Pargs='monotonic 40' -q

try.expect:
round robin, no token:
   1100 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1150 ms  r2     at position 1: pay-9 is authorized <- went back
   1200 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1250 ms  r2     at position 1: pay-9 is authorized <- went back
   1300 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1350 ms  r2     at position 1: pay-9 is authorized <- went back
  went back 3 times
with a session token (never below the highest position seen):
   1100 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1150 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1200 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1250 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1300 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
   1350 ms  r1     at position 2: pay-9 is captured
  went back 0 times

With the token, the session stays on its sticky follower, r1 here, and r2 would only be used if r1 died, and only once r2 had reached position 2. With r2 40 ms behind, round robin also goes back 0 times, because these reloads start 100 ms after the capture and both followers have it by then. A reload between 1,020 and 1,040 ms would still catch r2 without it: any two followers at different positions can produce the anomaly, and a smaller lag only narrows the window.

sections.h: Consistent prefix: effects must not show up before their causes
sections.html:
Inside one leader's log, a follower always shows a prefix of history: everything up to its position, in order, and nothing after it. If the authorization of pay-1 is position 40 and its capture is position 41, no follower can show the capture without the authorization. Single-leader replication gives you this for free.

It stops being free when related writes go into different logs. The Partitioning track splits big datasets into shards, and each shard has its own leader, its own log and its own followers. Nothing orders shard 0's log against shard 1's. Suppose the payments platform puts authorizations on shard 0 and captures and refunds on shard 1. Payment n is authorized at n × 50 ms and captured 30 ms later. Shard 0's follower is 400 ms behind, shard 1's is 20 ms behind. At 100 ms the fraud dashboard, reading both followers, sees pay-1 captured and no authorization anywhere, and raises an alert. In the lab, 201 refreshes over two seconds count 700 such sightings.

The guarantee is consistent prefix reads: if writes happened in a certain order, anyone who reads them sees them in that order, never an effect before its cause.

The fix is to keep causally related writes in one log. Shard by payment id instead of by event type, and a payment's authorization, capture and refund share one log, so any follower of that shard shows them in order. You already do this with Kafka: order holds only within a partition, so you key messages by payment id (the Messaging track's lesson on producers). It covers what shares the key. A merchant's daily total, built from many payments on many shards, can still be read at a moment when some shards are ahead of others.

The general fix is to track dependencies: each write carries the positions it depends on, one per shard, and a reader waits until its followers reach all of them. That is causal consistency, and the Consistency and consensus track builds it.

Anomaly What the user sees Fix What it costs
Read-your-writes own write missing token of own last write, or leader leader reads; a token per user
Monotonic reads data goes back in time sticky follower plus highest-seen token uneven load; reroutes
Consistent prefix effect before cause one log (shard key) for related writes key choice; cross-key order still open

figure.caption: Each shard's follower shows a prefix of its own log, but nothing orders the two logs. At 100 ms the dashboard sees a capture whose authorization is still on its way.

try.title: Shard by event type, then by payment
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. It writes 20 payments' authorizations and captures twice: once with a shard per event type, once with a shard per payment id, and counts captures the dashboard sees without their authorization.
Predict the count with -Pargs='prefix 20', where both followers are 20 ms behind. Is the problem the lag, or the two logs?

code.title: in the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l03.demo.AnomaliesDemoKt -Pargs='prefix' -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l03.demo.AnomaliesDemoKt -Pargs='prefix 20' -q

try.expect:
a shard per event type (shard 0's follower 400 ms behind, shard 1's 20 ms):
  at 100 ms the dashboard shows pay-1 captured, with no authorization
  captures without an authorization, summed over 201 refreshes: 700
a shard per payment (shard 0's follower 400 ms behind, shard 1's 20 ms):
  no capture ever appears before its authorization
  captures without an authorization, summed over 201 refreshes: 0

Each of the 20 captures is visible for 350 ms before its authorization arrives, and the dashboard refreshes every 10 ms: 20 × 35 = 700. With -Pargs='prefix 20' both lines say 0, because each capture is written 30 ms after its authorization and both followers are equally behind. Make the lags differ by more than 30 ms (prefix 60 counts 20) and the per-type sharding shows the anomaly again: the cause is two logs that replicate independently, and lag only decides how often you see it.

analogy: A news feed you follow on two devices, fed by two delivery trucks from one printing press. Read-your-writes: you posted a letter to the editor, and your own copy must include it even if the truck is late, so you pick up your copy at the press. Monotonic reads: you read Tuesday's paper on the phone, and the laptop must not hand you Monday's afterwards, so you stick to the truck you used, and if it breaks down you wait for one that has delivered at least Tuesday. Consistent prefix: the sports page and the front page come from two presses, and you must not read "Rovers celebrate the title" before "Rovers win the final", so stories that belong together are printed by the same press. The analogy breaks at what you carry: a reader knows the date on the paper, but a client only knows positions if the application hands them over.
world: Any Quarkus service that sends reads to an Oracle Active Data Guard standby or a PostgreSQL replica has these three bugs waiting, usually as "the record was just created and the next call returns 404". The cheap fix in a payments API is to return the commit's position (or a version number) with the write response and have the client send it back on the next read, then route by it. Temporal hits read-your-writes too: an activity that writes to the primary and a later activity that reads from a replica can run 5 ms apart on different workers, so the second must read from the primary or check the position. Kafka consumers rebuilding a read model are consistent-prefix machines: key every event by payment id, so an authorization and its capture land in one partition, in order. And give the dashboard's "Refund" button an idempotency key, because no read-routing trick protects the money as well as the database refusing the second refund.
mistake: Fixing read-your-writes with "read from the leader for N seconds after a write" and choosing N from the usual lag. It passes every test, because lag in tests is milliseconds. Then a follower restarts, replays for six minutes, and every user who wrote in that window sees their own data vanish, while the leader is also busy. People pick the time-based rule because it needs no plumbing: no position to capture, no token to carry. The fix is to compare positions, not clocks: capture pg_current_wal_lsn() (or the GTID, or MongoDB's operation time) at commit, carry it with the session, and route by pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= token, with a bounded wait and the leader as the fallback. Then alert on replay lag in bytes, so a follower that is far behind is taken out of rotation instead of serving stale data to everyone.

compare.title: Read-your-writes on PostgreSQL and on MongoDB

a.label: PostgreSQL (JDBC, Kotlin)
a.title: carry the LSN yourself
a.html: // after the write commits on the primary val token = primary.createStatement().use { st -> st.executeQuery("SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn()::text").use { rs -> rs.next(); rs.getString(1) } } session.lastWritten = token // stored with the user's session // before a read: is the standby there yet? val caughtUp = standby.prepareStatement( "SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= ?::pg_lsn" ).use { ps -> ps.setString(1, session.lastWritten) ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> rs.next(); rs.getBoolean(1) } } val conn = if (caughtUp) standby else primary

b.label: MongoDB (Java sync driver, Kotlin)
b.title: the session carries it
b.html: val session = client.startSession( ClientSessionOptions.builder().causallyConsistent(true).build() ) val refunds = db.getCollection("refunds") .withWriteConcern(WriteConcern.MAJORITY) .withReadConcern(ReadConcern.MAJORITY) refunds.insertOne(session, Document("paymentId", "pay-41").append("status", "requested")) // the driver sends the write's operation time as afterClusterTime; // a secondary waits until it has applied that far val mine = refunds.withReadPreference(ReadPreference.secondaryPreferred()) .find(session, Filters.eq("paymentId", "pay-41")).first()

compare.note: Both compare a log position with the follower's. With PostgreSQL you capture the LSN, keep it in your session store and decide where to read; the decision is in your code, so you choose the wait and the fallback. MongoDB's driver keeps the operation time in the session object and the server does the waiting, but only within one session object (pass it between requests, or store the operation time and use advanceOperationTime in the next session), and only with majority read and write concerns.

worked.title: A read router with a session token

steps.say: Keep the token with the user's session; a pooled connection serves many users. It holds two positions: the user's last write and the highest position any of the user's reads was served at.
steps.code: data class ReadToken(val lastWritten: Long = 0, val lastSeen: Long = 0) { val floor: Long get() = maxOf(lastWritten, lastSeen) // never read below this }

steps.say: After a commit, raise lastWritten to the commit's position. Any position that grows with the log works: an LSN as a number, a GTID count, an oplog time.
steps.code: fun afterWrite(t: ReadToken, commitPosition: Long) = t.copy(lastWritten = maxOf(t.lastWritten, commitPosition))

steps.say: Route: the sticky follower first, then any other at or past the floor, and the leader last. Count leader reads; that number is what the guarantee costs you.
steps.code: fun route(t: ReadToken, sticky: Replica, others: List<Replica>, leader: Node): Node = (listOf(sticky) + others) .filter { it.alive } .firstOrNull { it.position() >= t.floor } ?: leader.also { metrics.leaderReads.increment() }

steps.say: After the read, raise lastSeen to the position it was served at, so the next read can't go backwards.
steps.code: fun afterRead(t: ReadToken, servedAt: Long) = t.copy(lastSeen = maxOf(t.lastSeen, servedAt))

steps.say: Ship the token to the browser or store it per user, and send it back on every request. For a phone and a laptop, store it server-side by user id; a cookie only covers one device.
steps.code: HTTP/1.1 201 Created X-Read-After: 83895248 GET /refunds?payment=pay-41 HTTP/1.1 X-Read-After: 83895248

lab.title: Reproduce the three anomalies, then route around them
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder; no Docker. 14 of 18 fail. The 4 that pass already are the bug reports: they reproduce a missing refund, a payment page going back in time, sticky routing failing on a reroute, and 700 captures without an authorization, using only the given code. Read Lag.kt: a Replica's position at any moment comes from the log and its lag, and pause() freezes it like pg_wal_replay_pause().

Exercise 1, readYourWrites: read on the offered follower if it has the session's last write, wait for it if that takes at most maxWaitMs, otherwise go to the leader. ReadYourWritesTest includes a paused follower and the support agent whose token is 0.

Exercise 2, monotonicReads: never serve a session below the larger of its last write and its highest read, trying the sticky follower first. MonotonicReadsTest reloads pay-9 ten times, and SessionPropertyTest throws 200 random histories of lags, pauses, writes and reads at it.
Exercise 3, shardFor: put every event of a payment in the same shard. ConsistentPrefixTest counts what the fraud dashboard sees: 700 with a shard per event type, 0 with yours.
hints: readYourWrites: check replica.alive, then replica.position(now) >= session.lastWritten. If not, replica.reaches(session.lastWritten) is the moment it will be there, or null if it is paused below it; the wait is that moment minus now.

monotonicReads: val token = maxOf(session.lastSeen, session.lastWritten). Build the order as listOfNotNull(sticky) + replicas.filter { it.alive && it !== sticky }, then firstOrNull { it.position(now) >= token }, falling back to Route(leader).
If the property test fails, jqwik prints the seed and lags. Replay that seed in a plain test and print every Read it makes.

drill.title: Name the anomaly and its fix
drill.prompt: Without looking, for each case name the anomaly, then the fix with what it costs. (a) A customer changes their card's nickname and the next page shows the old nickname. (b) A chargeback analyst sees a dispute marked "won", reloads, and sees "open". (c) An audit view shows a refund for a payment that has no capture yet. Then write the one-line check a PostgreSQL router runs before reading on a standby.

answer.html:
(a) read-your-writes violation
    fix: carry the LSN of the customer's last write; read on a standby only when
    pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN, else wait briefly or read the primary
    cost: some reads go to the primary; the token must follow the user across devices
(b) monotonic reads violation
    fix: sticky standby per user plus a token of the highest position already seen
    cost: uneven load; a dead sticky standby needs a reroute that respects the token
(c) consistent prefix violation (capture and refund on different shards or logs)
    fix: shard or key both by payment id so they share one ordered log
    cost: the key must group everything that has to stay ordered

check:  SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= :token::pg_lsn;

recap: Asynchronous followers lag, usually by milliseconds and sometimes by minutes, with no bound. Eventual consistency only promises that copies converge once writes stop.
Each anomaly is a read served at a position behind something the reader already did or saw; each fix makes the reader carry a position and refuse to read below it.

Read-your-writes: keep the position of the user's last write (PostgreSQL LSN, MySQL GTID, MongoDB operation time) and read only from followers at or past it, with a bounded wait and the leader as fallback. remote_apply makes every commit pay instead.
Monotonic reads: a session never reads older data than it has already seen. Sticky routing gives it until the sticky follower dies; a highest-seen position makes it survive the reroute.
Consistent prefix: one log gives it for free; writes spread over shards lose it. Keep causally related writes in one log (key by payment id), or track dependencies, which is causal consistency.

explain.prompt: Your team lead asks why "just read from the replicas" caused three different kinds of bug reports, and why one fix covers two of them but not the third. Explain it.
explain.answer: The replicas copy the primary's log a little later, so each one is at some point in the past, and different replicas are at different points. Bug one: a merchant writes and immediately reads from a replica that hasn't got the write yet, so their own change looks lost. Bug two: someone reloads and lands on a replica that is further behind than the one they used before, so data appears to go back in time. Both happen because a read was served from a point earlier than something the user already did or saw. So the same fix covers both: we hand the user a position in the log, the position of their last write and the newest position they've read at, and we only serve their reads from replicas that have reached it, otherwise from the primary. Bug three is different: the fraud view shows a capture before its authorization because those two events live in different shards, each with its own log, and nothing orders one shard against another. No position in one log helps there. The fix is to put events that depend on each other in the same log, by sharding or keying them by payment id, or to track dependencies across shards, which is a bigger project.

deeper.html:
The four session guarantees come from a 1994 paper by Terry and colleagues on the Bayou system: read your writes, monotonic reads, writes follow reads, and monotonic writes. The last two are about writes: monotonic writes says your writes are applied in the order you made them, and writes-follow-reads says a write you make after reading something is ordered after what you read. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions promise all four with majority read and write concerns. Jepsen's consistency map shows where they sit: all four are implied by causal consistency, and all of them can stay available during a network partition as long as a client keeps talking to the same replicas, which Jepsen calls sticky available.

Bounded staleness is a different deal: instead of carrying a position, the client says "nothing older than 5 seconds". Azure Cosmos DB sells it as a consistency level, and DynamoDB's global tables document that a strongly consistent read can be stale if the item was last written in another Region. Time bounds are easy to state and hard to check, because a follower's idea of its lag in seconds depends on clocks (the Faults, time and truth track covers why that is fragile).

PostgreSQL has a second kind of "standby read waits": synchronous_commit = remote_apply with synchronous_standby_names, which makes the writer wait instead of the reader. And a quorum of standbys with ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3) plus remote_apply makes any of those standbys safe to read from after the commit returns. That is close to the "every replica is up to date" model that Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6 recommends when you can afford it: pretending that asynchronous replicas are synchronous is where these bugs come from.
